A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same distributional-unlearning framework. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison. Existing appendix content matches after renumbering; v4 adds Sections B.3–B.4.

before.justification: v3 reports original Gaussian simulations and CIFAR-10, Jigsaw and SMS Spam experiments in Section 4 and Appendix B, including forgetting, preservation and deletion-budget results.

after.justification: v4 retains these original experiments and adds CIFAR-10 feature-representation and coreset-comparison results in Tables 6–7.

M1.justification: The distance-based selection algorithm, top-f deletion and refitting procedure in Section 3, and scoring heuristics in B.2.1 are unchanged. Alternative feature extractors are tested in an ablation; the new budget-choice remark provides deployment guidance without revising the reported algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate synthetic Gaussians, CIFAR-10 cat-class removal, Jigsaw profanity removal and SMS Spam removal. The new experiments vary representations and comparators within the existing CIFAR-10 task. LLM applications remain proposed future work.

E2.justification: v4 substantially broadens the coreset comparison beyond v3's centroid-based and k-center heuristics by actually evaluating CRAIG, GradMatch and CCS at a matched 60% deletion budget in Table 7. This introduces gradient-based and coverage-based comparators while retaining the original comparisons. TDDS and UNSEEN are discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: B.3 introduces a controlled CIFAR-10 experiment varying the feature extractor among the default CNN, scratch/pretrained ResNet-18 and raw pixels, with selection and training otherwise fixed at 60% deletion. B.4 adds a matched 60%-budget baseline comparison. Existing splits, metrics and training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: B.3 adds a feature-representation sensitivity study, testing whether forgetting depends on the learned backbone or using raw pixels. This is a limited ablation on one dataset at one deletion budget. Existing supplementary analyses, including the Gaussian heuristic comparison in Figure 6, are retained.

E5.justification: Existing seed counts and standard-error reporting are unchanged. New Tables 6–7 continue the mean ± standard-error convention without specifying a changed repetition count or estimation procedure. B.4's significance wording does not introduce a documented statistical test.

E6.justification: Existing quantitative results are unchanged. New Table 6 reports forget accuracy of 21.6±1.9% with CNN features and 31.8±2.0% with raw pixels, alongside ResNet variants. Table 7 reports selective removal at 24.5±1.4%, versus random 39.2±1.9%, CRAIG 36.3±2.7%, GradMatch 35.5±4.2% and CCS 40.9±4.1%. These are additional comparisons, not established changes to previously reported same-setting performance.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, assumptions, bounds and Appendix A proofs are unchanged after matching numbering. In particular, v3's exponential-family Theorem 2 remains as Theorem 4 in v4. The new practical remarks introduce no formal theorem, derivation or revised guarantee.

C1.justification: The abstract narrows the exact Pareto-frontier claim from exponential families to Gaussian distributions. The broader exponential-family contribution remains in the introduction and appendix. The central selective-removal, sample-efficiency and deletion-savings claims are retained.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive discussion of noisy or proxy retain data, absent retain distributions, multimodal features and practical budget selection. It interprets the new feature and coreset results and discusses prospective LLM applications. Existing limitations concerning Gaussian assumptions, upstream sample identification and privacy evaluation remain.

D1.justification: Remark 2 adds practical budget-selection guidance using computational constraints or cumulative selection scores, and B.3 identifies the alternative feature extractors and their pretraining status. Existing B.2 implementation, hyperparameter and hardware details are unchanged. The additions provide little detail about coreset implementation or the pretrained ResNet source.

R1.justification: Sections 4.3 and 5 add focused discussion and references covering GradMatch, CCS, TDDS, UNSEEN and LLM instruction-data selection. These extend the existing distinction between single-distribution training-data selection and the paper's forget/retain objective, without redefining its fundamental research positioning.

P1.justification: v4 adds practical remarks, organizes the conclusion into named discussion paragraphs, appends B.3–B.4, adds acknowledgements and updates affiliations/contact information. The main narrative, section order and existing appendix prose are largely preserved.

P2.justification: Tables 6–7 are new, and Table 2 gains a separability column and explanatory caption text. Figures 3 and 4, previously stacked on one page, appear on separate pages. All six existing figures retain identical plot content; the overall visual format remains stable.

improvement.justification: Compared with v3's simple coreset comparisons and fixed feature representation, v4 adds more informative comparator evidence and directly tests representation sensitivity in Tables 6–7. Its discussion also clarifies practical reliance on retain data. These strengthen empirical support, but the additions cover one deletion budget, report only forget accuracy and provide sparse implementation details, limiting the overall gain.
